1:
What is told to open its doors is answered three ways. Gill takes Lebanon for the temple, built of its cedars. Henry reports the same reading and the story attached to it: the temple was burnt by the Romans and its gates forced open by the soldiers, and forty years before, the gates were said to have opened of themselves, whereupon a rabbi remarked that now he knew the destruction was at hand, by this very prophecy. Others understand it of the city, or rather the whole land, to which the mountain was an inlet on the north, so that all lies open. Wesley keeps the mountain itself, a northern boundary commanded to open the gates of the fortifications that secure its passes. Henry gives the summons a turn of his own: thou wouldst not open them to let thy king in, for he came to his own and his own received him not; now thou must open them to let thy ruin in.

Which destruction is meant is unsettled. Clarke says the chapter opens with the destruction of the city and polity, probably by the earlier empire, at least at first. Henry and Wesley take it of the later ruin of that church and nation, foretold in dark and figurative expressions and prophesied plainly by our Lord. Clarke then offers a second reading of the whole, scripture authorising it: the prophet, in the person of the Messiah, sets forth the ungrateful returns made to him when he took the office of shepherd, how they rejected him and valued his labours at thirty pieces of silver. He also sketches what follows: after breaking the two crooks that were the badges of his office, the prophet takes instruments made to hurt and destroy, expressing the judgments God would inflict by wicked rulers who destroy the flock and are destroyed themselves.

Calvin faces the inconsistency with what went before. The prophet has been encouraging the people to hope and declaring their condition would be so happy that nothing would be wanting; now he denounces ruin, saying God had long been the shepherd of that nation but renounced all care of them, wearied with a perverse wickedness he found in them all. These seem inconsistent, but it was needful first to set the benefits of God before them, that they might proceed with more alacrity in the building; and now necessary to change the strain, lest hypocrites confiding in the promises should be hardened, and lest the faithful should not entertain due fear. He adds the purpose of such threatenings: that any who might repent should be restored by fear, the reprobate left inexcusable, and the faithful fortified against despondency. Keil and Delitzsch describes the same movement: the Lord rescues his people from the world-powers, and then, because it repays his pastoral fidelity with ingratitude, gives it up to the foolish shepherd, who will destroy it and himself fall under judgment; by this addition an abuse of the promise of salvation is prevented.

Whether the trees are men or houses divides them. Gill takes the fir and the cedar for the princes and magistrates, noting a paraphrase that interprets them of kings and princes; Clarke reads the same clause of the fall of all the mighty men. Wesley takes them for what was made of them, houses built with fir, oaks used for palaces and fortresses, and the forest for the city itself, called so for its many tall houses. On the next verse Gill allows two senses, the civil rulers, as a paraphrase and two Jewish expositors take it, or the ecclesiastical; Clarke makes the young lions princes and allows either kings or priests for the shepherds. Wesley alone keeps the picture literal, the shepherds howling because the enemy has driven away their flocks, and the pride of the river being the forests on its banks where the young lions ranged.
4:
Who is commissioned is agreed by three voices. Gill says the words are not the prophet's but the Messiah's, who calls the Lord his God as man and Mediator, what follows being the Father's words giving him a commission; Wesley says the same in a line. Henry puts it as typology, that the prophet is made a type of Christ as an earlier prophet sometimes was, and that the scope is to shew Christ came into this world for judgment, and for judgment to a church and nation wretchedly corrupted at the time of his coming by the worldliness and hypocrisy of their rulers; he would have healed them, but they would not be healed, and are therefore left desolate.

The name given the flock is glossed three ways. Clarke says the people resemble a flock fattened for the shambles, and takes the command to feed them as a command to instruct a people about to be slaughtered. Ellicott makes the participle present, a flock being slaughtered. Wesley makes it a flock appointed to slaughter, and counts four hundred and fifty years in which that people were such a flock to three successive powers.

Who the possessors are is the sharpest question here. Gill rules out one answer expressly: they are not the later conquerors, by whom great numbers were slain without its being accounted a sin, but the priests and scribes and doctors among the people themselves, who ruined their souls with poisonous doctrines, teaching the commandments of men and the traditions of the elders, and bidding them seek salvation by the works of the law, all the while thinking they did God good service. Henry says the same at length: their slavery at home made them as miserable as captivity abroad, and in the prophet's own time the nobles were rebuked for exacting usury of their brethren while the governors oppressed the people through their servants. Later the chief priests and elders, who were the possessors of the flock, became perfect tyrants by their traditions and their impositions on men's consciences, devoured their houses and fleeced the flock instead of feeding it, one party corrupting the people's judgments and the other their morals by making void the commandments of God; and in all this they justified themselves, slaying the sheep and holding themselves not guilty. Clarke identifies them as governors and false prophets, who slay the flock by leading them into what brings destruction, and says those who sell them give them up to idolatry and then bless God, strange to tell, that they profit by the establishment of a false religion. Wesley calls them governors who sell the people for slaves and profanely thank God for thriving by cruelty. Ellicott adds a textual note, that the possessive in the clause about their shepherds is a gloss of the English version.

How wide the threat runs is disputed as flatly. Ellicott takes it as universal, preferring the world to the land and mankind to the men, and explains that God would punish the nations for their cruelty to his people and cause the world to be broken up with wars and civil tumults. Gill keeps it local, that God will no more spare the inhabitants but cause his wrath to come upon them to the uttermost, as when the city was destroyed. Wesley reads the delivering into a neighbour's hand as a licence to rob, imprison, banish or kill one another, and identifies the king named as the foreign ruler that people had themselves chosen, whose armies would destroy the land. Clarke names a different power, saying God had determined to deliver them into the hands of the earlier conquerors. Keil and Delitzsch marks where the narrative turns, that from the next verse the feeding of the flock is described, and renders its object the wretched ones of the sheep, with the two staves named Favour and Bands.
7:
The two staves are read as tools by one voice, as tokens by another. Clarke takes them literally, as two crooks with distinct offices: the first probably the one by which the sheep were marked, its end dipped in vermillion, used when every tenth sheep was set apart; the second the one with a hook at the head, by which the shepherd caught a sheep by the leg to bring it to hand. Ellicott takes the same names as tokens: he would render the first favour rather than beauty and the second binders rather than bands, the one denoting the return of God's favour and the other the binding of the two houses in brotherhood, which happened for the first time since their separation at the return from exile. He also corrects the tense, that the prophet fed the flock rather than will feed it, acting as God's representative in a symbolical action.

Who the three shepherds are is the great crux, and Gill and Clarke both work through a list. Gill sets aside a series of proposals: three figures of the exodus suggested in the Talmud, three of the first king's house who died within a short space, three later kings who fell by their enemies, the three last prophets, and three brothers of a fighting house. He inclines to the three sects among the people, though some substitute one sect for another and some the scribes, and others think the three courts of judicature are meant; his own preference is the three orders of magistrates, princes, prophets and priests. Clarke canvasses the same field, three brothers of that house, three wicked high priests, or the three last princes of a royal line, and settles like Gill on three orders rather than three men, the priesthood, the teachers and the magistracy, all annihilated at the conquest.

Ellicott approaches it through the month rather than the men. The period seems to him symbolical, so that taking a day for a year one month means about thirty years; some take one month for a short time simply, which agrees with his view. Others take each day for seven years, making thirty days two hundred and ten, and identify the shepherds with three empires of about that span; but he answers that no instance can be cited in which a prophetic day equals seven years. On his own reckoning the three may be kings of a Greek dynasty who fell within a generation, one dying miserably abroad, one put to death by a rival, the rival overthrown in his turn. As specimens of attempts to keep the month literal, he cites one early writer for kings, priests and prophets, and a modern one for priests, judges and lawyers who, having delivered the Saviour to the cross, were taken away within one month.

The withdrawal that follows is a turning away. Gill takes it of a feeding that stops, the shepherd having fed them in his public ministry and afterwards by his apostles, who were sent to that people first but on being despised were ordered to turn to the nations; this shews, he says, that not the shepherds only but the body of the people abhorred him and his gospel. Clarke gives the sentence in three parts, that he will instruct them no longer, some appointed to death by famine, others to the sword, others to such desperation that they destroy one another. Wesley reads it as following the patient feeding and the cutting off of the unfaithful shepherds, and glosses the last clause two ways: either they live to be besieged until hunger makes the living eat the dead, or by seditions they destroy each other. Keil and Delitzsch notes that with the breaking of the first staff the shepherd withdraws one side of his care but has not yet ended his connection with the flock.
10:
What the first staff stands for is answered four ways. Gill takes the staff for the gospel, which cannot itself be made void, since it endures till all the elect are gathered in; but it may be taken from one people and given to another, generally through contempt and unfruitfulness, and that is what happens here, the gospel going into the Gentile world. Clarke reads it of their standing, that the shepherd would no longer preserve them in their free and glorious state, breaking a covenant they had broken already. Ellicott reads it of a covenant made not with them but for them: the people having rejected him, he broke the staff Favour and annulled the covenant made with the nations on their behalf, preferring nations to people; and dates it at the close of a victorious period, when the nation was corrupted and harassed on every side. Wesley makes the staff the covenant of God with its blessings, which Christ calls his own because he was the mediator of it. On when the breaking took place Gill distinguishes three moments: in right on the day Christ died, apparently when the substance of the gospel was removed, in fact at the destruction of the city.

The demand for wages is a test. Ellicott says the shepherd demands a requital as a test of the sheep's gratitude, and takes the alternative offered seriously: God does not force our will, which is free, but sets life and death before us, so that by his grace alone we can choose him, though we can refuse both his grace and himself. Wesley reads it as a reckoning at parting, the shepherd putting it to them whether he had deserved anything at their hands; the weighing was the manner of paying money then, and the sum named the value of a slave's life. Clarke calls the rating contemptuous; Gill fixes who is addressed, not the poor of the flock but the others who despised him.

Where the money is thrown divides them. Ellicott says the price was so contemptible that it is flung to the meanest of craftsmen, and thinks the phrase probably proverbial for throwing anything worthless away; the old Greek, he notes, by the change of a single letter read the treasury for the potter. He renders the next clause ironically, an exclamation at the magnificence of the price the speaker was valued at, and pictures the prophet flinging it to a potter where the covenant had been ratified by sacrifice, so pronouncing the divorce. Wesley says the sum was so little it would hardly purchase anything but the cheapest ware, and prefers to render it that the money is cast into the house of the Lord for the potter. Clarke reports a writer who supposed the price is cast to the humblest of the temple ministers, those who furnished its earthen vessels; he himself reads it as give him any price, since neither betrayal nor crucifixion could happen without the speaker's permission.

The second staff breaks for the same reason. Keil and Delitzsch says that after this shameful payment the shepherd breaks it as a sign that he will no longer feed the ungrateful nation but leave it to its fate, the breaking being interpreted by the staff's name, of destroying the brotherhood between the two houses. Gill allows three senses: the removal of civil government, the abrogation of the older law, or the ordinances of the gospel. Ellicott dates the breach late, from the civil discords after a period of victory to the siege of the city. Clarke reports a writer who cannot explain the passage without supposing the northern kingdom still standing when the prophet wrote, referring the words to the wars between the two kingdoms or to the captivity in which the brotherly connection ceased. Wesley keeps the typology: the prophet did it in the type, Christ really.
15:
Whether the implements differ at all is asked outright. Clarke assumes they do: a bag without bread, a scrip without measure, a staff without a hook, things of no use, pointing at pastors who never cared for the flock. Henry says the same, accoutrements no way fit for the business, such a coat and bag and staff as a foolish shepherd would appear in. Ellicott declines the question: it is needless to inquire in what respects, if any, these instruments differed from a wise shepherd's, since the words merely imply that the prophet, having represented one character, should now personate the other. Wesley puts it in a line, to personate a shepherd quite different from the one already represented.

Who the foolish shepherd is draws a long list of rejections from Gill. He places him not in that land but in the empire, and sets aside two named kings of the region, a Greek persecutor, the priests who governed after the prophet's time, the scribes and Pharisees, the general who destroyed the city, and a false Messiah; one writer, he reports, takes the words of the emperors who followed the one under whom Christ was crucified. Clarke keeps it vaguer, some wicked king, reporting a writer who names a northern one. Ellicott makes it not a man but a class, all the misrulers of the nation from the decline of a glorious period to the day when they declared they had no king but Caesar. Henry divides the oppression into three: unfaithful ministers, whose doctors by their traditions make the law more a yoke than God made it; unmerciful princes, to whom, having rejected him by whom princes decree justice, they were justly turned over; and false prophets.

The catalogue of neglects is glossed clause by clause; Ellicott prefers the scattered to the young one. Wesley takes them in order: the shepherd seeks not the lost, neglects the young as aptest to perish, leaves the wounded to die, and passes by what cannot go forward, while he feasts on the fattest and tears their skin to the nails; a sluggish and cruel government is shadowed out by such a shepherd. Keil and Delitzsch gives the same list as a rendering, what is perishing he will not observe, what is scattered he will not seek, what is broken he will not heal, and marks that this comes after the good shepherd is compelled to lay down his office.

The closing woe is read for its two organs. Gill takes the title as the shepherd of nothing, an idol being nothing in the world. Clarke and Ellicott render it worthless or useless, Clarke adding that he is shepherd in name but does not do the work, Ellicott that though allowed for a time to neglect the flock, the judgment of God falls on him in the end. On the sword Clarke assigns each member a meaning, the arm the secular power and the right eye the ecclesiastical state, so the withering of the one is the breaking of that power and the darkening of the other the restraining of prophecy, the whole state so eclipsed that none of its functions can be performed. Wesley moralises the same two: they who should have been workmen and were slothful will have their arm dried up, and they who should have been watchmen and were drowsy will have their eye blinded. Ellicott closes with a proposal about the text, reporting a scholar who maintains that a passage in a later chapter is out of place and should be moved to the end of this one. He finds apparently some truth in it, since the summons to the sword against the shepherd seems to follow naturally here, and meets the objection that the phrase about God's fellow would be strong for a foolish shepherd by replying that all shepherds, good or bad, are reckoned God's ministers.
